Visual Data Story of Parking Patterns at Carlaw Student Village

The Daily Flow of Carlaw Student Village

Understanding how parking capacity fluctuates is crucial for student residents. To figure out exactly what’s going on, I spent a few weeks tracking how many cars were parked in the lot at different times. By looking at the average number of cars for each day of the week, we can get a basic idea of when the lot is completely packed.

A bar chart titled ‘Average Car Count by Day of Observation’. The x-axis lists the days of the week from Monday to Sunday. The y-axis shows the average cars observed. The steel blue bars indicate the varying average parking lot occupancy levels throughout the week.

Comparing Rhythms: Weekdays vs. Weekends

Just looking at daily averages doesn’t tell the whole story, though. an 8:00 AM on a Tuesday has a completely different vibe than an 8:00 AM on a Saturday. By breaking the data down into specific time chunks and splitting it into weekdays versus weekends, the real patterns start to show up. These boxplots let us see exactly how parking traffic shifts.

A side-by-side boxplot comparing car counts across six specific time intervals, from 2 am to 10 pm. The boxes are color-coded: blue for Weekdays and orange for Weekends. The chart shows the median, quartiles, and outliers of parking traffic for each time block, highlighting the differing patterns between week days and weekends.

Behind the Scenes: The Observation Effort

somebody actually had to go out and collect all this data. Instead of looking at the cars, this heatmap shows my schedule—basically, when I was actually out there logging the observations. The numbers in the grid show how many times I recorded data for each time slot, which gives a cool little look into the human side of actually doing this project.

A visual table heatmap titled ‘Logging Activity Frequency’. The y-axis shows the days of the week, and the x-axis shows the time intervals. Cells contain bold text numbers indicating exactly how many observations were logged during that specific period, with the background color lightly shading from white to light blue to emphasize higher counts.
